title: Air India CEO Summoned Over Immigration Lapse as Leadership Arrives at Bombay House
excerpt: The Centre has summoned Air India chief Tewolde Gebremariam over the departure of three Italian nationals from Delhi without immigration clearance, as he and predecessor Campbell Wilson arrived together at Bombay House in Mumbai.
body:
• The Centre has summoned Air India CEO and MD Tewolde Gebremariam over an alleged immigration lapse in which three Italian nationals departed Delhi's IGI airport without mandatory departure immigration clearance.
  • Gebremariam and his predecessor Campbell Wilson arrived together at Bombay House, the Tata Group headquarters in Mumbai, as the summons landed on Tuesday, September 15.
  • The September 12 show-cause notice from the Ministry of Civil Aviation called the episode a "serious security and immigration-related lapse" and gave the airline seven days to respond.
  • Initial reports point to a ground-handling error: the three passengers carried "D"-marked domestic boarding passes on the Amritsar-Delhi sector but were routed through international-to-international transfer instead of domestic arrivals.

Mumbai/New Delhi, September 15, 2026 — The Centre has summoned Air India's top leadership over the airline's handling of an alleged immigration lapse that allowed three foreign nationals to depart India without completing mandatory immigration checks, intensifying government scrutiny of the Tata Group-owned carrier just as a new chief executive takes charge.

Air India Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director Tewolde Gebremariam and his predecessor Campbell Wilson arrived together at Bombay House — the Tata Group's headquarters in Mumbai — on Tuesday, just as the summons reached the airline, according to ANI. The pairing was symbolic as well as practical: Wilson has formally handed over the CEO and MD role to Gebremariam, who took charge earlier this month after the Air India board announced the leadership transition last month.

"Air India and India have been a wonderful experience. It's been a privilege to be part of Air India's long and proud history," Wilson told reporters, adding that he was happy to be handing over to Gebremariam as his successor and wishing the airline well in its rise to become a world-class carrier, according to the ANI report.

"Air India and India have been a wonderful experience. It's been a privilege to be part of Air India's long and proud history."

— Campbell Wilson, outgoing CEO and MD of Air India

Context & Background

The summons follows a show-cause notice issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) on September 12, which termed the incident a "serious security and immigration-related lapse" and sought a detailed explanation of the circumstances that led to the breach, sources told ANI. The airline was given seven days to respond.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=a5CwU9gyqxc

According to the notice, three Italian nationals arrived at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport at 12:50 am on September 4 on Air India flight AI-1115 from Amritsar, then boarded Lufthansa flight LH-763 to Munich at 1:45 am without obtaining mandatory departure immigration clearance, businessline reported. The ministry said the incident occurred during Air India's hub-and-spoke operations and involved a violation of the prescribed standard operating procedure (SOP).

An initial report attributed the lapse to ground-handling procedures, industry sources told businessline. The passengers' boarding cards carried a "D" marking, identifying them as domestic passengers on the Amritsar-Delhi leg. They should have been directed through domestic arrivals, exited, and then re-entered via international departures to complete immigration formalities — but were instead allegedly directed through international-to-international transfer procedures, a route that allowed them to reach the Lufthansa counter without departure immigration checks.

Impact & Analysis

The summons marks a sharp escalation: a show-cause notice is a regulatory instrument; summoning the CEO personally signals that the government regards the breach as a security matter, not just a compliance slip. The Home Ministry has already treated it as one, convening an emergency meeting chaired by Home Secretary Govind Mohan on September 15 with officials from civil aviation, the Intelligence Bureau, the Bureau of Immigration, Air India, and Delhi airport.

The timing compounds pressure on the airline's leadership transition. Gebremariam inherits the crisis days into his tenure, and the optics of arriving at Bombay House alongside Wilson on the day of the summons suggest the Tata Group wants a unified, senior-level response. Earlier this month, Air India Chairman N Chandrasekaran told employees at an internal meeting that restoring trust must remain the airline's foremost priority, requiring "world-class processes, rigorous compliance and personal accountability across the organisation," according to industry sources cited by ANI.

"The most important thing Air India should aspire to have is trust in the minds of people. Air India must be known for caring about safety above everything else."

— N Chandrasekaran, Chairman of Air India

The incident also exposes a structural vulnerability in Indian airports' domestic-to-international transfer flows. Hub-and-spoke operations — where passengers from feeder cities like Amritsar connect to long-haul international flights in Delhi or Mumbai — rely on ground staff to route passengers correctly between terminals and transfer channels. A single misdirection, in this case allegedly by the ground-handling agency, bypassed an entire layer of border control. For regulators, that is a systems failure worth answering for at the highest level.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora — millions of whom transit through Delhi and Mumbai on precisely these Amritsar-Delhi or similar feeder connections to reach North America, Europe, and the Gulf — the episode is a reminder that immigration procedures are a two-way gate. The government's response signals that departure lapses will be treated as seriously as arrival violations, which matters for travelers who assume a boarding pass and a checked-through bag mean every formality is handled.

Diaspora travelers with complex itineraries — domestic legs booked separately from international connections, short transfer times, terminal changes — are the most exposed to exactly this kind of routing error. The safe habit remains unchanged: even when connecting on the same airline, confirm with staff which immigration and transfer channel applies before following an escort or signboard.

What's Next

Air India's seven-day window to respond to the show-cause notice runs until September 19, and the CEO's summons suggests the government wants answers beyond a written reply — potentially in person. The Home Ministry's emergency review may recommend changes to transfer-area SOPs, additional checks at international transfer desks, or penalties for the ground-handling agency involved.

For Gebremariam, the first test of his tenure will be whether the airline can present a credible account of what went wrong and what it is fixing — and whether the Tata Group leadership, convening at Bombay House, is willing to back that account at the highest level. The Videshi will continue tracking this story.
